claims.text: Hardness in BCC high-entropy alloys is governed by interactions between edge dislocations and HCP-element-induced lattice distortion.
Strength in BCC high-entropy alloys is governed by interactions between edge dislocations and HCP-element-induced lattice distortion.
Increasing the concentration of HCP elements causes significant changes in lattice distortion, dislocation-core structure, and slip behavior in BCC refractory high-entropy alloys.
Edge dislocations can be prevalent and can control plastic flow in a BCC high-entropy alloy.
The proposed controlled material has a single-phase BCC initial structure.
Introducing HCP elements is the intervention intended to change lattice distortion and dislocation behavior.
Edge dislocations undergo thermal super-jogging at elevated temperature.
Thermal super-jogging of edge dislocations increases barriers to dislocation motion.
The edge-dislocation mechanism produces approximately temperature-independent strength from 673 K to 1073 K.
The NbTaTiZrV0.5 high-entropy alloy exhibits an unusual strength plateau between approximately 673 K and 1073 K.
The modified alloy will retain high yield strength and ultimate tensile strength within the proposed temperature interval.
An otherwise similar alloy without HCP elements is an appropriate baseline for isolating the HCP-element effect.
Above 1073 K, diffusion-controlled deformation mechanisms become active.
Activation of deformation mechanisms above 1073 K softens the alloy.
A significant decrease in yield strength and ultimate strength above 1073 K would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly predicts softening above 1073 K, whereas the falsification rule says that the same decrease in yield and ultimate strength above 1073 K would falsify the hypothesis. Thus, the proposed falsifying observation is actually an expected observation.
